title: H-1B and H-2B visa programs: documented cases
label: Documented cases and program weaknesses. Correlation, not proof of cause.

h1b_approvals.units: H-1B petitions approved by USCIS per fiscal year (regardless of when filed)
h1b_approvals.note: Approved petitions, not people: one worker can have several petitions. 'Initial' = new H-1B employment with an employer (only some count against the cap); 'continuing' = extensions, amendments, employer changes. FY2001 is not shown because the official FY2001 report could not be retrieved for verification. FY2020+ figures use USCIS's revised (first-decision) method, so they are not perfectly comparable with earlier years. FY2025 is a total only, from a different USCIS report table.

cap.text: Annual cap: 65,000 regular H-1B visas plus 20,000 for holders of U.S. master's or higher degrees (85,000 total). Universities, affiliated nonprofits and government research organizations are exempt, and the cap does not apply to continuing-employment petitions. The cap was temporarily higher in FY1999-2000 (115,000) and FY2001-2003 (195,000).

sources.label: USCIS, H-1B Specialty Occupations (cap and exemptions)

china_shock.text: Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2016) report that import growth from China between 1999 and 2011 led to an employment reduction of 2.4 million U.S. workers (including local demand and reallocation effects), versus a 2.0 million job-loss estimate for national industries and 985 thousand within manufacturing (direct plus input-output exposure). These estimates come from Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson & Price (2016), summarized in the review. Economists debate the overall size and net effect.

sources.label: Autor, Dorn & Hanson, 'The China Shock: Learning from Labor-Market Adjustment to Large Changes in Trade', Annual Review of Economics 8 (2016); NBER WP 21906
Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson & Price, 'Import Competition and the Great US Employment Sag of the 2000s', Journal of Labor Economics 34(S1) (2016)

cases.title: GAO-11-26: H-1B Visa Program: Reforms Are Needed to Minimize the Risks and Costs of Current Program
cases.text: GAO found program oversight 'fragmented and restricted', no legal provision holding employers accountable when they obtain H-1B workers through a staffing company, and statutory changes that 'increased the pool of H-1B workers beyond the cap and lowered the bar for eligibility'. Fewer than 1% of employers garnered over one-quarter of all H-1B approvals (FY2000-2009).

cases.title: DOL Office of Inspector General, Report 06-20-001-03-321
cases.text: OIG found the Wage and Hour Division 'cannot initiate investigations unless it receives a complaint from an aggrieved party or a credible source', and the Secretary's authority to initiate H-1B investigations had never been used, which 'can prevent DOL from holding H-1B program violators accountable'.

cases.title: DOJ & DOL settlements with Facebook: up to $14.25 million
cases.text: DOJ's Civil Rights Division alleged Facebook preferred temporary visa holders over qualified U.S. workers for PERM-related (green-card) positions, Jan 2018-Sep 2019. Facebook agreed to a $4.75 million civil penalty and up to $9.5 million for eligible workers. Facebook denied the allegations.

cases.title: DOJ settlement with Apple: up to $25 million
cases.text: DOJ's Immigrant and Employee Rights Section found Apple did not advertise PERM positions on its external job site and required mailed paper applications, deterring U.S. applicants (2018-2019). Apple agreed to $6.75 million in civil penalties and an $18.25 million back-pay fund. Apple disputed the findings.

cases.title: Southern California Edison IT outsourcing
cases.text: Computerworld and the Los Angeles Times reported about 500 SCE IT jobs cut (about 400 layoffs plus about 100 voluntary departures) as work moved to Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services; workers said they trained their H-1B replacements. SCE said it complied with the law; DOL later closed its Infosys inquiry with no violation found (Reuters, Sep 8 2015).

cases.title: Walt Disney World IT layoffs
cases.text: The New York Times reported that about 250 Disney IT workers in Orlando were laid off in 2015 and that many were required to train foreign replacements on H-1B visas brought in by an outsourcing firm. Reuters reported the firm was HCL Technologies and that DOL was reviewing complaints (Sep 8 2015).

debate.text: Economists disagree about H-1B's overall effect on U.S. wages.

sides.label: EPI (Costa & Hira, May 4 2020)
sides.text: 60% of H-1B positions certified by DOL in FY2019 were at the two lowest prevailing-wage levels (Level 1 = 17th percentile, Level 2 = 34th percentile), below the local median wage.

sides.label: Peri, Shih & Sparber (Journal of Labor Economics, 2015)
sides.text: Across 219 U.S. cities (1990-2010), H-1B-driven growth in foreign STEM workers was associated with faster wage growth for college-educated native workers and no significant effect on native employment.

h2b.title: H-2B (non-farm seasonal work, incl. landscaping and construction)
h2b.text: H-2B lets employers hire foreign workers for temporary non-agricultural jobs (66,000 per fiscal year by statute, plus supplemental visas some years). The documented H-2B abuses below are mostly employers underpaying and intimidating the H-2B workers themselves, which also undercuts the wage floor for U.S. workers in the same jobs. Annual H-2B visa counts since 2000 (State Department) are not charted yet: the State Department statistics site blocked automated download from our build box, so we show no number rather than an unverified one.

cases.title: DOL: New York landscaping company to pay $1.1M after overtime, H-2B program violations
cases.text: DOL's Wage and Hour Division found Dario's Landscaping (Southampton, NY) failed to pay overtime, gave investigators false records, failed to pay H-2B workers the correct rate (Oct 2018-Oct 2021), threatened workers who cooperated and coached false testimony. Total $1.1 million for 54 workers plus civil penalties; debarred from H-2B for one year.

cases.title: DOL: Haverhill, MA company violated temporary visa worker program; $832K for 47 landscaping workers
cases.text: DOL's Wage and Hour Division recovered $832,000 in back wages and damages for 47 landscaping workers (per DOL news release).
